beginner: Leeks like deep, loose, rich soil with lots of compost worked in. Loose soil matters because you grow the long white part of a leek by pulling soil up around the stem, and that is much easier in soft, crumbly ground than in heavy clay. Keep the soil evenly moist all season.
seasoned: Work in generous compost or rotted manure before planting and aim for a deep, loose, fertile, well-drained bed. Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders with a shallow root system, so the soil must hold both moisture and nutrients near the surface across many months; loose ground also makes the repeated earthing-up that blanches the shank far easier.

beginner: Leeks grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test takes out the guesswork. If your test comes back below about 6.0, adding garden lime brings it up.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN gives 6.0 to 7.0; UF/IFAS lists 6.5 to 7.0 for Florida). Leeks tolerate a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band but dislike strongly acid ground; below about 6.0 a liming amendment helps. Confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

beginner: Leeks grow for a long time and are fairly hungry plants. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed once or twice with a nitrogen fertilizer through the summer while the stems are growing. Steady feeding builds thick stems. Do not pile on a lot of fertilizer late in the season, since soft, crowded, well-fed plants get rust more easily.
seasoned: Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (UMN suggests about one cup per 10 feet of row mid-season), then side-dress with nitrogen once or twice while the shafts are lengthening. USU gives a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet in the middle of May and again in late June. Keep nitrogen steady through summer for thick shanks, but avoid heavy late feeding, which together with crowding and wet leaves worsens leek rust.

beginner: Feed your leeks some nitrogen now to grow thicker stems.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your leeks with nitrogen to push shaft growth.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once or twice during summer.
seasoned: A balanced base such as 10-10-10 at planting, then nitrogen side-dressings (for example ammonium sulfate, 21-0-0) through summer to build long, thick shanks.

beginner: About a quarter pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate for every 100 square feet each time you feed, or follow the package directions.
seasoned: About a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet at each side-dressing (USU), or roughly one cup of 10-10-10 per 10 feet of row mid-season (UMN), or the label rate of a balanced fertilizer.

beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down where the leaves fold together. They are worst in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf folds and the tight neck of the shaft; heavy feeding in hot, dry spells weakens plants and slows shaft growth.

seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry weather and shelter deep in the leaf folds where sprays miss them; weak, drought-stressed leeks are hit hardest.

beginner: Keep the plants healthy and well watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant leeks where you grew onions or leeks last year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.
seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and evenly watered, hose off light infestations, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.

seasoned: Pale, papery window-pane patches where caterpillars have eaten the inner leaf tissue, then tunnels bored down into the shaft; two generations feed roughly May to June and August to October.

seasoned: Larvae of the leek moth (Acrolepiopsis assectella), a small brown moth; young caterpillars mine the foliage and older ones bore into the stems, then pupate in net-like silk cocoons spun on the leaves.

beginner: Cover the plants with fine insect netting during late spring and late summer when the moths are active, move leeks to a new spot each year, and squash any little net-like cocoons you find on the leaves.
seasoned: Cover the crop with insect-proof mesh through the flight periods, rotate alliums, and find and crush the white net-like cocoons on the foliage.

seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue left in the ground.

beginner: Do not plant leeks where alliums grew recently, clean up old plant debris, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.
seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull plants and crop residue, and use floating row cover at establishment to block egg-laying.

seasoned: The allium leaf miner (Phytomyza gymnostoma), an increasingly widespread fly with two generations a year, active roughly March to April and again September to November; secondary rots often follow the tunneling.

beginner: Cover the plants with fine insect netting in spring and again in fall when the flies are active, and move leeks to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Cover the crop with insect-proof mesh during the two flight periods (about March to April and September to November) and rotate alliums, since the flies emerge from pupae in the soil.

seasoned: Bright orange pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces that break open to a dusty spore powder; severe infection shrivels leaves early and saps vigor, common from mid-summer into late autumn.

beginner: A fungus that causes orange rust. It spreads in damp, humid weather and is worse when plants are crowded or pushed with too much nitrogen.
seasoned: The fungus Puccinia porri (formerly P. allii); it is worse on crowded plants, in humid weather, and on nitrogen-rich, low-potassium soils.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, do not over-feed with nitrogen, pull off and bin badly spotted leaves, and clear away old leaves after harvest. Pick rust-tolerant varieties if you can.
seasoned: Space plants for airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, balance feeding, remove and destroy badly infected leaves and post-harvest debris, and choose more rust-tolerant varieties where available.

seasoned: Yellowing, dieback, and wilting starting at the leaf base, with a fluffy white mold and tiny poppy-seed-like black sclerotia at the base and roots; affected plants pull up easily.

beginner: A soil fungus that attacks onions, garlic, and leeks. Its tiny resting bodies can live in the soil for more than 20 years and wake up when allium roots are near.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Stromatinia cepivora (Sclerotium cepivorum), whose sclerotia survive in soil for over 20 years and germinate in response to allium roots; even a few sclerotia per soil sample can start the disease.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. Start with clean plants, keep infested soil off your tools and boots, and do not rely on rotation alone, because this fungus lives in the soil for decades.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Plant only clean stock, practice strict sanitation to avoid moving infested soil, and note that rotation alone will not control it because the sclerotia persist so long.

seasoned: Roots turn pink, then red, and shrivel, stunting plants and shortening shafts; most common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.

beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when onions and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year, especially in warm soil.
seasoned: A soilborne fungus that builds up in continuous allium ground and is favored by warm soil; stressed plants show it worst.

beginner: Rotate where you plant leeks, start with clean healthy transplants, and keep the plants well cared for so they are not stressed.
seasoned: Rotate away from alliums for several years, start with clean transplants, and keep plants unstressed and evenly watered.

beginner: Water leeks regularly so the soil stays evenly moist the whole time they grow. Their roots are shallow, so dry spells make the stems shorter and tougher. Unlike onions, you do not stop watering at the end.
seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist across the whole long season; leeks are shallow-rooted and any drought check shortens and toughens the shaft. They do not need a dry-down at the end the way bulb onions do.

beginner: About an inch of water a week is a good target, and more during hot, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
seasoned: Aim for about an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation (USU advises moistening the soil to a depth of about 18 inches every seven days), more in heat or sandy soil, delivered steadily.

beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent rust.
seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; lingering leaf wetness and humidity feed leek rust.

beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Sitting in wet soil makes leeks rot.
seasoned: Waterlogged soil with yellowing, mushy bases signals overwatering; standing moisture around the shaft encourages basal and white rots.

beginner: Wilting, bluish, or brown-tipped leaves mean the leeks are too dry. Leeks that do not get enough water make thin, short, tough stems.
seasoned: Bluish, wilting, or tip-burned leaves and stalled growth mean the plants are short of water; under-watered leeks make thin, short, fibrous shanks.

beginner: Keep the soil surface damp while the tiny leek seeds sprout, usually indoors. Do not let them dry out partway through coming up.
seasoned: Keep the surface continuously moist as the fine seed germinates, usually indoors in trays; leek seed is small and slow and should not dry mid-germination.

beginner: Keep the young leeks evenly damp as they grow to about pencil thickness before you plant them out. Steady water now makes stronger plants.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with even moisture until they reach pencil thickness for transplanting; steady watering builds the strong roots that transplant well.

beginner: After dropping the seedlings into their deep holes, water them in and keep the soil evenly damp. The shallow roots need steady water to get growing.
seasoned: Water the seedlings in at transplant to settle the deep planting hole, then keep the bed evenly moist; shallow leek roots need steady moisture to establish and start the shaft.

beginner: As the white stems get longer through summer and fall, keep the water steady, about 1 inch a week soaking deep. Letting them dry out makes short, tough leeks.
seasoned: Shaft lengthening through summer and early fall is the most water-sensitive phase. Never let the bed dry out while the stems bulk; USU advises moistening to about 18 inches every seven days. Drought here shortens and toughens the shaft.

beginner: Leeks do not need to dry out before harvest the way onions do. Keep watering evenly right up to when you dig them, and they hold in the ground into winter.
seasoned: Unlike bulb onions, leeks need no dry-down at the end. Keep steady moisture right through harvest; leeks stand in the ground into winter and stay tender when kept watered until dug.

beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to get rust.
seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for leeks because lingering leaf wetness and humidity are exactly what leek rust needs.

beginner: If you grew your own seedlings indoors, set them outside for a few hours a day for about a week before planting so they get used to sun and wind. Plant them when they are about as thick as a pencil and around 8 inches tall.
seasoned: Harden off greenhouse or windowsill seedlings with about a week of gradual outdoor exposure before set-out. Transplant when seedlings are pencil-thick and roughly 8 inches tall; trimming the tops and roots back slightly at planting is a traditional aid that is optional.

beginner: Most gardeners start leeks from seed indoors about 10 weeks before planting out, because they grow slowly and need a long season. In mild areas you can also sow seeds straight in the garden. To plant a seedling, make a hole about 6 inches deep with a dibber, drop the seedling in, and just water it; the soil washes in on its own. Planting deep like this starts the long white stem.
seasoned: Two entry points: start seed indoors about 10 weeks before set-out for transplants (the usual approach, since leeks are slow and long-season), or direct-sow in mild, long-season areas. Transplant into a deep dibble hole about 6 inches deep and water gently so soil washes in around the seedling without filling the hole; this sets the seedling deep and starts the blanched shank. Drop the transplant in and do not pack soil around it.

beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer under the pot. Leeks should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil around the base leads to rot.
seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; leeks must never sit in standing water, which saturates the shaft base and invites rot.

seasoned: A deep, free-draining potting mix blended with compost.

seasoned: Leeks are cold-hardy enough to stand in a deep container and be harvested through winter in mild-winter zones. In colder zones, group pots against a wall or mulch them, since a container root zone chills faster than open ground.

beginner: Leeks grow in pots if the pot is deep, because the long white stem needs depth. Use a container at least 12 inches deep with drainage holes, and space plants about 4 to 6 inches apart. Pots dry out fast, so check the soil often and keep it evenly moist, or the stems stay short.

Containers dry fast and the crop is long, so water before the surface crusts and feed steadily; interrupted growth makes thin, short shanks. You can mound mix up the stems in the pot to blanch them just as in the ground.

beginner: Do not plant leeks where you grew onions, garlic, or other leeks recently. Some allium diseases live in the soil and build up, and white rot can last over 20 years. Wait at least 3 to 4 years before growing alliums in the same spot again.
seasoned: Avoid following leeks or other alliums (onions, garlic, shallots) in the same ground; several allium diseases, including pink root and especially white rot, persist in soil, white rot for over 20 years. A home garden can target at least 3 to 4 years between allium crops.

beginner: Leeks do well planted after leafy greens or beans and peas. Just do not plant beans or peas right next to leeks, since alliums can slow them down.
seasoned: Leeks follow well after a leafy or legume crop. Like other alliums, they are traditionally kept away from beans and peas, which alliums are thought to inhibit.

beginner: Leeks do not keep at room temperature. The best way to store them is to leave them growing in the garden and dig them up as you need them.
seasoned: Leeks are not a long-keeping crop and do not store at room temperature. The best storage is to leave them standing in the garden and harvest as needed; lifted leeks soften quickly in a warm room.

beginner: In the refrigerator, trimmed leeks last about one to two weeks, best wrapped so they do not dry out. They keep best cold and humid.
seasoned: Trimmed leeks keep about one to two weeks in the refrigerator, ideally wrapped to hold moisture; USU notes they hold best in cold (32 to 40°F), humid conditions.

beginner: You can slice leeks and freeze them. They go soft after thawing, so use frozen leeks in cooked food like soups, not in salads.
seasoned: Leeks freeze well sliced; texture softens, so use frozen leek in cooked dishes such as soups and stews rather than raw.

beginner: The simplest way to keep leeks is to leave them in the garden, because they handle frost and stand through winter. In very cold areas, pile mulch over them or dig them up and tuck them into damp sand or soil somewhere cold and sheltered.
seasoned: The classic way to store leeks is in the ground: they are cold-hardy and stand through frost, so in much of the country you simply leave them and harvest into winter. In the coldest zones, mulch heavily over them or lift and heel them into damp sand or soil in a cold, sheltered spot.

beginner: The fast early leek: it sizes up in about 85 days from transplant, giving tall, tender stems for late summer and fall. King Richard is less cold hardy than the winter types, so plan to use it before hard freezes rather than leaving it standing through winter.
seasoned: An early, quick-sizing summer-to-fall leek, about 85 days from transplant (Cornell trial). It is the tender member of the set, best used before hard freezes rather than overwintered. Useful for a first harvest while the maincrop and overwintering types size up behind it.

beginner: A reliable, vigorous maincrop leek for fall harvest, about 100 days from transplant. Lancelot is widely adapted and hardy enough to stand into cold weather, which makes it a good first choice if you are not sure what to grow.
seasoned: The default maincrop pick: vigorous, uniform, and widely adapted, about 100 days from transplant (Cornell). Hardy through fall and light freezes, though not bred to overwinter like Bandit or Giant Musselburgh. If you grow one leek, grow this one.

beginner: A dependable open-pollinated standard, also sold as Broad London, with thick shanks for fall harvest in about 120 days from transplant. It is the classic home-garden leek that Utah State and other extension guides still recommend.
seasoned: The old open-pollinated standard (sold as Broad London), thick-shanked and dependable for fall, roughly 120 days from transplant. Hardy into cold weather; a maincrop workhorse rather than a dedicated overwinterer. USU-listed.

beginner: A hardy, uniform leek that holds well as the weather turns cold, about 110 days from transplant. Tadorna bridges the gap between the fall maincrop types and the true overwinterers, so you can keep harvesting into early winter.
seasoned: A hardy, uniform Dutch maincrop, about 110 days from transplant (Cornell trial), that stands well into cold and bridges the fall-to-overwintering window. Tougher than the plain fall types but stops short of Bandit or Giant Musselburgh for deep-winter standing.

beginner: The toughest overwintering leek here: a very cold hardy, blue-green type (the Blauwgroene Winter strain) that stands in the garden through winter into spring in milder zones. It is slow and late, about 120 days from transplant, but it is the one to grow to dig leeks fresh in the cold months.
seasoned: A very hardy, blue-green overwintering leek (Blauwgroene Winter, RHS AGM as Bandit), late and slow at about 120 days from transplant (Cornell trial) but the most weather-tough of the set. It stands hard winters into spring where the class is viable; the headline overwinterer.

beginner: A hardy old Scottish heirloom with broad, mild shanks that takes cold well, about 110 days from transplant. It is a traditional pick for a winter standing crop, an open-pollinated alternative to Bandit if you want to save seed or grow a heritage variety.
seasoned: A broad-shanked Scottish heirloom, open-pollinated, very hardy and traditional for a winter standing crop, roughly 110 days from transplant. The heritage overwinterer alongside Bandit: milder flavored, a touch faster, and seed-saveable.

beginner: Pick a leek by when you want to harvest. Early types like King Richard grow fast for late summer and fall but are less hardy. Maincrop types like Lancelot or American Flag give the main fall crop. Overwintering types like Bandit or Giant Musselburgh are tougher and slower, made to stand in the garden through winter so you can dig them up fresh in the cold months. Unlike onions, leeks do not care about day length, so just match the type to your season.
seasoned: Choose by season first. Early or summer types (King Richard) are fast and tall but less hardy, for late-summer and fall use. Maincrop types (Lancelot, Large American Flag, Tadorna) carry the main fall harvest. Overwintering types (Bandit, Giant Musselburgh) are slower, shorter, and blue-green but the most cold-hardy, bred to stand in the ground through winter into spring. Matching variety to how late you want to harvest matters far more for leeks than for onions, since leeks have no day-length requirement.

beginner: Leeks are easygoing neighbors. Their strong allium smell is traditionally said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and they tuck in nicely beside celery, beets, and lettuce. The main thing to avoid is planting them next to beans or peas, which alliums can slow down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things.
seasoned: Leeks earn their companion reputation mostly through scent, traditionally credited with masking carrots from the carrot rust fly, so the classic leek-and-carrot pairing is the best known. They also share a long cool-season bed comfortably with celery, beets, and lettuce. The firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep leeks away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions.

beginner: Leeks and carrots are a classic pair. The strong onion-family smell of leeks is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two do not crowd each other.
seasoned: Leeks and carrots are the textbook allium-and-umbellifer pairing. The leek's sulfur scent is traditionally credited with masking carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two have complementary upright forms that share a bed without crowding. Treat the pest benefit as a plausible tradition rather than a proven effect.

beginner: Celery and leeks both like the same rich, moist soil and long cool season, so they make easy, undemanding neighbors.
seasoned: Celery and leeks are a traditional bed pairing built on shared culture: both want deep, rich, evenly moist soil and a long cool season, and both are often trenched or earthed up, so they fit the same management. The benefit is compatibility and efficient use of a rich bed, not a documented pest or growth effect.

beginner: Keep leeks away from beans and peas. Onions and their relatives, including leeks, are thought to slow the growth of these legumes.
seasoned: Alliums, including leeks, are traditionally held to inhibit beans and peas, so the long-standing advice is to keep them apart. The mechanism is debated and the effect is not firmly demonstrated, but it is a consistent enough tradition across the onion family to respect as a low-cost precaution.

beginner: Look for thin, grass-like shoots, each starting bent over in a little loop like a hairpin, then standing up. Leeks sprout slowly, so do not worry if they come up over a week or two rather than all at once.
seasoned: A single looped seed leaf pushes up bent like a hairpin, then straightens into the first slender grass-like blade. Leeks germinate slowly and unevenly over cool to moderate soil, so stands come up over a week or two.

beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the tiny seeds do not dry out, and pull weeds early. If you planted young plants instead of seeds, you can skip this stage.
seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so the fine seed never dries mid-germination, and keep seedlings weed-free; young leeks compete poorly. If you set transplants, this stage is already behind you.

beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts leeks next time.
seasoned: Note your sowing date and first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next season.

beginner: The seedlings grow slowly into thin, upright plants, getting to about pencil thickness and 8 inches tall over a couple of months, usually indoors. Be patient, this is just how leeks grow.
seasoned: Slow, thin, upright seedlings build toward pencil thickness and about 8 inches tall over roughly 8 to 10 weeks, usually indoors or in a nursery bed. This is a patient stage; leeks are deliberate growers.

beginner: Keep the seedlings in bright light, water them evenly, and feed a little. Grow them until they are about as thick as a pencil before planting out.
seasoned: Keep seedlings in good light, evenly moist, and lightly fed. Grow them to pencil thickness before transplanting; a stronger seedling makes a thicker shaft later.

beginner: Note how long the seedlings took to reach planting size. It helps you time your indoor start next year.
seasoned: Track sowing-to-transplant time; leeks reward a full, unhurried seedling stage with bigger plants.

beginner: After you plant the seedling deep in its hole, it settles in and starts growing upright again. The base is sunk deep in the soil, which is what starts the long white stem.
seasoned: After set-out into a deep dibble hole, the transplant roots in and resumes upright growth. Early leaves green up and the base sits deep in its hole, the start of the blanched shank.

beginner: Plant each seedling in a deep hole and just water it, letting the soil wash in on its own. Keep weeds out and the soil moist while the plants settle.
seasoned: Plant into a 6-inch dibble hole and water without filling it, so soil washes in gradually. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist while plants take hold.

beginner: Write down when you planted out and how far apart. It helps you plan next year.
seasoned: Note your transplant date and spacing; it anchors the long run to harvest.

beginner: Through summer and early fall the plant grows lots of leaves and the white stem gets longer and thicker. This is the main growing time, helped by steady water, feeding, and pulling soil up around the stems to keep them white.
seasoned: Through summer and early fall the plant stacks leaves and the white shaft lengthens and thickens. This is the main growth phase, driven by steady moisture, feeding, and repeated earthing up to blanch the stem.

beginner: Keep watering and feeding, and two or three times pull loose soil up around the stems to grow a longer white part. Add only an inch of soil at a time and keep it below where the leaves split.
seasoned: Feed and water steadily, and earth up the stems a couple of times, drawing loose soil up around them (never more than an inch at a time, and not over the leaf joint) to lengthen the blanched white shank.

beginner: Note when you fed and hilled the soil up. Comparing that to how long the white part got helps next year.
seasoned: Log feeding and earthing-up dates against final shaft length; it tunes your blanching routine.

beginner: The white stems reach about an inch or more across and the leeks are ready. Leeks handle frost, so you can leave them in the ground and dig them up fresh from fall into winter instead of all at once.
seasoned: Shanks reach about an inch or more across and the leeks are ready. Because they are cold-hardy, they hold their quality standing in the ground through frost, so harvest runs from fall into winter as needed rather than all at once.

beginner: A leek is a mild, sweet relative of the onion, but instead of a bulb you grow and eat the long white stem. Leeks take a long time, so most gardeners start them indoors in late winter and plant them deep, then pull soil up around the stems to keep the bottom part white and tender. The best thing about leeks is that they handle cold: they stand right in the garden through frost and even taste sweeter for it, so you can dig them up fresh from fall into winter instead of all at one time. Which leek you plant sets how late you can harvest: fast early types like King Richard are for late summer and fall, while very hardy overwintering types like Bandit and Giant Musselburgh are bred to stand out in the cold and be dug through winter.
seasoned: Leek (Allium ampeloprasum) is the mild, sweet allium grown not for a bulb but for its long, thick, blanched white stem, or shank. It is a patient, long-season crop, usually started indoors in late winter and transplanted deep so soil can be earthed up around the stem to blanch it. Its great virtue is cold-hardiness: leeks stand in the garden through hard frost, sweetening with the cold, and are dug fresh from fall into winter rather than harvested all at once. There is no bulbing and no day-length requirement, so unlike onions you simply match the variety to how late you want to harvest: an early tender type like King Richard for summer and fall, hardy maincrop types like Lancelot through the fall, and very hardy overwinterers like Bandit or Giant Musselburgh to stand through winter into spring.

beginner: Leeks are ready when the white stem is about an inch or more thick. You do not have to wait for an exact size, and smaller ones are fine too. Loosen the soil with a fork and lift them out gently. Since leeks handle frost, leave the others in the ground and dig them up fresh from fall into winter as you need them.
seasoned: Leeks are ready once the white shank is about an inch or more across and several inches long; there is no need to wait for a set size, and you can begin earlier for slim leeks. Lift by loosening with a fork rather than pulling. Because they are cold-hardy, leave the rest standing and harvest from fall into winter as needed.

beginner: Leeks fall into two camps by how much cold they take. Summer and early types, like King Richard, grow fast and are meant to be eaten in late summer and fall; a hard freeze will damage them, so harvest before deep winter. Overwintering types, like Bandit and Giant Musselburgh, are bred to stand right in the garden through winter and be dug fresh in the cold months. How far north you can overwinter one depends on your zone: the hardiest leeks shrug off temperatures around 20°F and lower, and a thick mulch of straw or leaves buys roughly another zone of protection. In the coldest areas, treat even a hardy leek as a fall crop, or harvest and store it before the ground freezes solid.
seasoned: Leek cold tolerance sorts into three classes the app uses to judge overwintering viability by zone. Tender types (King Richard) are grown in season and harvested by fall; they are not overwintered. Hardy maincrop types (Lancelot, Large American Flag, Tadorna) stand through fall and light freezes and overwinter in milder zones, roughly zone 7 and warmer, a zone lower under mulch. Very hardy types (Bandit, Giant Musselburgh) stand hard winters, roughly zone 5 to 6 and warmer, again hedged with mulch and snow cover. UMN reports some varieties take temperatures near 20°F without harm, and RHS confirms hardy winter leeks stand the coldest weather unprotected, sweetening with frost. These are hedged ranges, not hard cutoffs: microclimate, mulch, and a hard-freeze year all shift the line, so the model states viability as a range and leaves the per-zone call to the app.
